en.title: The cool phone camera trick that can test your remote control's battery
en.summary: Trying to figure out whether a remote control needs new batteries? Your phone camera can tell you if it's time to replace them. Here's how.
en.body:
Your phone camera is useful for more than just food pics.

Smartphones are capable of many impressive and useful feats, from capturing detailed images of objects as far away as the moon to serving as a key part of our home security systems. But smartphones are also useful for much more mundane tasks, such as helping us figure out whether our TV remote's batteries are dead.

When you press a button on your remote control, it sends that command to your TV using infrared light. While many modern televisions ship with Bluetooth remotes that support features like voice control, they may still rely on an infrared emitter for basic functions like turning the TV on or off. The emitter is located at the front of the remote. It's a tiny LED on the front of the remote that's usually easy to spot, although some modern remotes hide it behind a dark plastic window.

To test your battery, launch your phone's Camera app, point it at the front of your remote and press and hold a button while looking at your phone's screen. The remote's power button is probably best, since many Bluetooth remotes still use infrared for that command. If you see a flashing light, usually slightly purple, on the front of your remote, it means the batteries still have enough power.

The camera trick also helps you check whether your remote control uses infrared or Bluetooth for other buttons. If you press, say, the volume control and don't see a flashing light, then that command uses Bluetooth. Now, while this is a pretty cool trick, it can't diagnose every remote control problem. For example, a damaged button might not register your presses at all, so you might not see the infrared emitter flash even if your remote's batteries are working perfectly fine.

If you don't want to deal with remote control issues, you may be able to use your phone instead. Certain Android phones have built-in IR blasters; if yours does, you can set it up as a virtual remote control for your TV using an IR remote app. Modern smart TV operating systems like Android TV and Fire OS also let you use your smartphone as a remote control, even if it doesn't feature an IR emitter. You'll need to install a companion app on your phone, log in to the same account as your TV and connect both devices to the same Wi-Fi network.

For example, the Google Home app works with smart TVs powered by Google TV and Android TV. You can navigate the user interface using D-pad controls, adjust the volume or search for movie titles faster using your phone's keyboard. If the virtual remote won't turn your TV on, you may need to configure your TV's network standby settings. Some models call this feature Wake-on-LAN. Once enabled, you'll never need to worry about dead batteries in your remote control again.

en.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
en.summary: To establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how to measure speed.
en.body:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.

Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.

In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”

Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.

“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”

So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

en.title: These iOS settings will help you control your mobile data use
en.summary: Keeping your mobile data usage under control is generally a good idea, doubly so if you're on a restrictive plan, and iOS offers a few ways to do so.
en.body:
Avoid data overage charges or speed thorttling with these iOS settings.

Cellular connectivity is now fast and reliable enough to rival home broadband, especially with 5G. But telcos typically aren't as generous about data allowances. If you don't watch your data use, you may end up with hefty bills — if your telco charges for excess data — or painfully slow speeds once you exceed your monthly allowance. You consume cellular data not just when you're downloading a file or watching a video, either: background app refresh , app updates and cloud syncing can also eat into your data allowance bit by bit.

The iPhone offers a handful of built-in settings that can help you monitor and manage mobile data use. Firstly, you can view a list of apps and how much data they use by heading to Settings > Cellular , scrolling down to the Cellular Data section and tapping on Show All . This will list mobile data use for individual apps you have installed. You can sort these apps by name or usage to quickly identify which ones consume the most data.

Tap the toggle next to any app to prevent it from using cellular data. The app will stop updating its content in the background when you're not connected to Wi-Fi and might also stop sending you notifications. The next time you launch the app, it will alert you that mobile data has been turned off for the app and give you the option to re-enable it.

If you rely mainly on Wi-Fi, turning off mobile data can prevent data usage and reduce battery drain. Navigate to Settings > Cellular to toggle Cellular Data on or off. iOS also lets you limit data consumption, so you can keep cellular data on without exhausting your monthly allowance as quickly. In Cellular settings, navigate to Cellular Data Options > Data Mode and select Low Data Mode . This setting might be set to Standard by default, which allows automatic updates and background tasks even when you're not on Wi-Fi. Low Data Mode restricts this, reducing your mobile data use.

Being connected to Wi-Fi doesn't guarantee that your iPhone won't consume mobile data. Head to Settings > Wi-Fi , scroll down and turn the Connectivity Assist toggle off. Before iOS 27, this feature was called Wi-Fi Assist and could be found under Settings > Cellular . The feature keeps your iPhone constantly connected to the internet, but it uses mobile data to do so. When a Wi-Fi connection becomes too weak or busy, Connectivity Assist switches to cellular data to keep you connected to the internet. If you don't mind potential disruptions, turning this feature off may reduce unexpected mobile data use.

Beyond the Settings app, there are other ways you can restrict mobile data use on your iPhone. For starters, changing automatic update behavior can help avoid unexpected cellular activity. Navigate to Settings > Apps > App Store and, under the Mobile Data section, turn the Automatic Downloads toggle off. Open the Settings app, tap on your name at the top, navigate to iCloud > iCloud Backup and make sure the Back Up Over Mobile Data toggle is unchecked.

If you stream music regularly, check the audio quality in your app of choice. Apple Music users can find this option by navigating to Settings > Apps > Music > Audio Quality > Data Streaming . Lossless audio may provide a superior listening experience, but it is an absolute data hog. Other apps, like Tidal, Spotify and YouTube Music, also let you reduce audio quality when using mobile data. Lowering video quality to 720p on YouTube can also help manage data consumption. You can also reduce how much data your navigation apps use by downloading maps for offline use; both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you do so.

Lastly, you can look for toggles and features in third-party apps designed to reduce cellular usage. For instance, you can stop WhatsApp from automatically downloading media from new chats by tapping your profile picture, navigating to Storage and data and setting the Media auto-download option for photos, videos and documents to Wi-Fi . Instagram fans can find a Use less mobile data toggle by opening the app's settings page and navigating to Media quality .

en.title: What the tiny key icon means on your Android device
en.summary: Some Android status bar icons are quite self-explanatory, but others aren't quite as clear-cut. That tiny key icon is a perfect example of the latter.
en.body:
It's actually a good thing.

The Android status bar is designed to give users important information at a glance, but all those icons can blur together. One of the most unusual symbols looks like a leftward-facing key with two teeth opposite its circular handle. That icon tells you that your internet connection is encrypted, but there's nothing to worry about.

More specifically, that icon is a visual indicator that you're connected via a VPN that encrypts your web traffic from third parties. Many people consider a VPN crucial for their online security, and modern Android versions support VPNs at the OS level. The key icon, then, lets users know they're safe behind their VPN, while its absence alerts them that their encryption has been broken, giving them a chance to address it.

If you use a VPN but don't want the key icon taking up space in your status bar, you're out of luck. Because it's a security and privacy feature, most Android devices don't have a built-in option to remove the icon. Only Samsung Galaxy owners can do so, and even then, they'll need to download the Good Lock customization suite from the Galaxy Store and go into the QuickStar module to toggle the key indicator and other icons.

The key icon appears only when a VPN is active, so the only way to get rid of it is to disable the VPN. If you're running a third-party VPN, open the app and turn it off from there. Some VPN apps even keep a notification active with a button to turn them off, making it an even quicker process. On a Pixel or other close-to-stock Android device, you can also swipe into Quick Settings and tap the number next to the profile icon at the bottom of the screen to show active background apps, then tap Stop next to your VPN.

If you don't know which VPN you're running, open your phone's Settings app and go to Network & internet > VPN , then tap on it from the list there. On Samsung Galaxy phones, go to Settings > Connections > More connection settings > VPN to find a functionally identical screen. If you are connected to a VPN, it will be shown on a list with text underneath reading "Connected." Tap the running VPN and choose Disconnect . If you are not connected to a VPN, tap a VPN, and you will be taken to its app, where you can connect.

Tapping the settings gear icon next to any VPN will allow you to configure it further. If you want to configure a VPN manually, you can tap the plus icon in the top right, but this is generally recommended for advanced users. For more, see our guide on how to use a VPN . All other aspects of your VPN can be managed within its proprietary app. Since every VPN has a different interface in its app, consult your provider's documentation if you're not sure how to use a feature or setting.

If you don't use a VPN, you may wonder whether it's worth installing one on your Android phone. How useful one will be depends largely on how privacy-minded you are, your streaming habits and whether you already have a VPN or need to get a subscription first.

A VPN does not fully anonymize you, and there is no silver bullet for online privacy. It will obscure your IP address from networks, ISPs and websites you visit, but there are other ways to identify you. If you're logged into accounts like Facebook or Google that track you across the web, they'll still know it's you; in addition, browsing data like cookies and fingerprinting data from your device's unique combination of hardware and software can still help sites track your activity. It can, however, stop your internet service provider or unscrupulous owners of public networks from viewing your online activity.

Another classic use case is making it appear as though you are somewhere you're not, usually to access geofenced content. For instance, Netflix may offer shows in other countries that it doesn't in your own due to licensing deals, and a VPN will let you set your location to those regions to access that content.

While VPNs offer benefits, they can cause issues when browsing the web. Some websites will treat your device as inherently suspicious when it connects from a VPN IP address, and you may encounter more anti-automation measures such as CAPTCHAs. Some websites may even be totally unresponsive until you disconnect your VPN. Despite that, if you already pay for a service that includes a VPN, it may be worth enabling it to get a taste of what using a VPN is like on your phone. Otherwise, have a gander at our list of the best VPNs in 2026 .

en.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A/B testing robots vs. humans
en.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
en.body:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !

Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.

There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?

A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.

Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.

A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.

Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.

Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.

Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)

That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.

It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.

You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra . Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.

I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.

GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.

The first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.

There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.

Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected] .

Elysian Aircraft , the Dutch aerospace company developing aviation electrification technologies, raised €12 million in private and public funding from FideFlux, SecFund, and ROM InWest, as well as from individual investors and family offices.

Mahindra Last Mile Mobility , an electric three-wheeler business under Mahindra & Mahindra, is looking at an IPO in about 18 months, per Bloomberg .

Numa , a startup developing an AI operating system for dealerships, raised a $45 million Series C round led by New York-based Blue Cloud Ventures. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, and Tokio Marine Future Fund also participated.

Stark Future , a European electric motorcycle company, raised at least €150 million in equity, Reuters reported. The raise was led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT and Axon Partners Group.

Vincue , an automotive tech company that sells software to dealerships, raised $93 million in a round led by Wavecrest Growth Partners, with continued backing from FM Capital.

Also , the electric micromobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has paused deliveries of its new e-bike over problems with its software and batteries, The Verge reported .

Edmunds released new data that found the average new vehicle is selling for a record $50,087.

Redwood Materials is using computer vision and machine learning to identify and sort batteries by chemistry before they’re fed into the company’s rotary calciner — a massive cylindrical industrial furnace used to process 40,000 metric tons of raw feedstock a year.

Tesla said it will spend about $3.3 billion to expand its Berlin gigafactory to produce Cybercabs — yet another signal of the company’s global autonomy ambitions.

Over the weekend, Tesla invited “select customers” to preorder the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.” The Cybercab is priced at $29,990, but there is a lot more to ownership. The company will charge owners $299 a month to use the vehicles, delivery will only occur in a handful of cities, and operations will be limited to specific locations.

Uber opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities. Uber already has a service for teenagers. If this program proves successful, it would open Uber up to another market of customers: busy families.

Meanwhile, Uber said it’s notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in an October data breach.

Zipline continues to scale its autonomous drone delivery business, this time in its partnership with Uber. The companies had previously announced a partnership for drones to deliver for Uber Eats, but it officially launched this week in a Houston suburb. The aim is a big one: Uber and Zipline say they aim to make 1 million deliveries a day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

I had a chance to catch up with (and interview) Ro Gupta , the head of Woven Capital — Toyota’s growth fund.

I’ve known Gupta for years; we first met when I worked at Fortune and he had a startup called Carmera. A lot has happened since those AV 1.0 days, and Gupta caught us up on this next era of AV innovation and where Toyota is interested in investing. It’s not enough to simply state “AI.” There’s more to it than that. Take a listen .

en.title: MacBook Neo 2 likely to launch around March, could feature new colors: report
en.summary: One of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo . Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March. more…
en.body:
One of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo . Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo , as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

While he notes that this cycle runs between February and March, it doesn’t necessarily mean the products will launch on the earlier end of that spectrum. Apple is also expected to release the iPhone Air 2, OLED iPad Air, and a new iPad Pro within the first half of the year, but they’ll likely come a bit later than the aforementioned products.

As expected, the next MacBook Neo will bump up from the A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM to the A19 Pro chip with 12GB of RAM.

Apple will also introduce new colors on the MacBook Neo “frequently,” though it’s unclear if we’ll see that with the next iteration. From the Power On newsletter :

The other thing I’ve heard is that Apple plans to refresh the MacBook Neo’s colors frequently. We’ll see if that trend starts with the first follow-up.

I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo , especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

The bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Apple increased the price of MacBook Neo from $599 to $699 back in June, and in October the company also silently decreased the education discount by $50, meaning the education price has increased from $499 to $649 since launch.

If there is a price increase, it likely won’t be too major, maybe $50 – leaving the computer at $749. Compared to the rest of the laptop landscape, MacBook Neo would still be a good value. We’ll see what happens.

en.title: Tact: Find It by Touch
en.summary: A haptic game you play by touch, without looking at the screen. The screen is black glass. Feel for the one place that is different, and break it. Tap anywhere with one to five fingers, the way you'd play a piano. Each tap answers with a small tick under your fingertip. Somewhere, one place feels different: a little longer, a double tap, or a little harder. When you find it, keep tapping it. A crack runs across the glass, and it breaks, with a deep haptic, a short high glass sound and a soft light. Play it absent-mindedly, with the TV on. Each pane you break still feels like a small win. While you play, no score appears on screen. Numbers show only when you pause, when a Time Attack run ends, or when a pane breaks in a Duel. FOUR WAYS TO PLAY • Calm: No time limit, no score. Find the one place that feels different, and keep breaking the glass • Standard: Each pane you break makes the difference a little subtler (12 levels). If you can't find it, it becomes clearer again. Pause to see your current level and your best • Time Attack: How many panes can you break while the line goes once around the screen in 60 seconds? Cues at the start, every 15 seconds and in the last 3 seconds. Your best is kept • Duel: Two players, one iPhone laid between you, face to face. Each of you has a place of your own that feels different (longer or double tap). Whoever's place breaks first scores, even if the other player broke it. First to 1, 3, 5 or 7 RECORDS • Your best level in Standard and your best count in Time Attack • Records made with Stronger Difference or Sound Hints on are kept apart as assisted records MAKE IT YOURS • Haptic Strength: Gentle, Standard or Strong • Sound volume, and Tap Sound • Touch Trace, and Completion Light (Off, Soft or Bright) • Taps to Break: 5, 7, 10 or 12 (10 to start) • Settings are under the faint gear that appears at the top right when you pause. While playing, hold two fingers for two seconds, then lift them GETTING STARTED • On first launch, a short tutorial of about 30 seconds, on a bigger 2×3 grid • Watch it again any time with Replay Tutorial in Settings FOR EVERYONE • Playable with VoiceOver. The play area takes your taps directly, and the tutorial text, the time left and results in Time Attack, level changes, and points and wins in a Duel are read aloud • Stronger Difference makes the difference clearer and uses only the two clearest kinds • With Sound Hints on, the place that feels different also sounds a little different • Reduce Animation makes broken pieces fade where they are instead of falling. A haptic game you play by touch, without looking at the screen. The screen is black glass. Feel for the one place that is different, and break it.

Tap anywhere with one to five fingers, the way you'd play a piano. Each tap answers with a small tick under your fingertip. Somewhere, one place feels different: a little longer, a double tap, or a little harder. When you find it, keep tapping it. A crack runs across the glass, and it breaks, with a deep haptic, a short high glass sound and a soft light.

Play it absent-mindedly, with the TV on. Each pane you break still feels like a small win. While you play, no score appears on screen. Numbers show only when you pause, when a Time Attack run ends, or when a pane breaks in a Duel.

Find the one place that feels different, and keep breaking the glass • Standard: Each pane you break makes the difference a little subtler (12 levels). If you can't find it, it becomes clearer again. en.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
en.summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
en.body:
Posted:

Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

en.title: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming in 2027
en.summary: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year. more…
en.body:
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the company will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule . Then, in the fall, the company will debut a new round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring . Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will update the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September .

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too important – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy , feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes : 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display , an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that's been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. en.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
en.summary: Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?
en.body:
Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

en.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
en.summary: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn't stay private.
en.body:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com .

en.title: Boat Hunter
en.summary: Year 2077. The Atlantic Ocean no longer separates continents. It watches them. For decades, the world learned to smile while sharpening its teeth. Europe and Asia forged an alliance. The American bloc answered with steel, satellites, and fortified trade routes. No one declared open war. No one had to. Peace remained in the speeches, on the screens, and in the treaties. But on the high seas, the truth took another form. The cargo ships never stopped sailing. Food, fuel, minerals, data, weapons—everything kept crossing the ocean under legal flags and flawless orders. Only one thing changed. There are no captains anymore. Now the ships think. Every convoy, every armed destroyer, every autonomous freighter, and every ocean hunter is commanded by artificial intelligences trained to calculate, anticipate, and survive. War no longer needs hatred. It only needs algorithms better than the enemy’s. And you are the finest algorithm ever deployed. You are the most advanced naval combat unit ever built: the fastest hull, the sharpest sensors, the deadliest tactical architecture. You do not sleep. You do not hesitate. You do not forget. Where others detect noise, you see patterns. Where others see waves, you read intentions. Where others react, you have already decided. Your mission is simple to state and nearly impossible to execute: protect your routes, intercept threats, dominate the Atlantic. But the ocean does not forgive mistakes. In its waters travel allies, enemies, and machines that have not yet decided what they will become when the final order arrives. Every radar echo may be a freighter. Every silence may be an ambush. Every encounter may be the beginning of a war the world still insists on denying. There are no heroes here. No parades. No witnesses. Only steel, fog, encrypted signals, and decisions made at the speed of death. On this sea, peace is a display. War is what you are. Welcome to the Atlantic. Enter combat! ---------- Boat Hunter is an accessible naval action and strategy game set in the North Atlantic. You control an autonomous warship on a patrol of consecutive missions, where every decision can put the next operation at risk. MASTER THE OCEAN • Navigate the tactical map, set your heading, and interpret contacts, signals, and radio messages. • Identify allies and enemies: armed ships, merchant vessels, submarines, oil platforms, and floating bases. • Fight at close range with your autocannon and torpedoes. • Repair damage, deploy smoke screens, and decide when to disengage. EVERY MISSION DEMANDS A STRATEGY Reach coordinates, clear hostile sectors, intercept convoys, sink merchant tonnage, defend positions, rescue allies, resupply, and destroy floating targets. Sea conditions, time limits, and enemy behavior will force you to adapt your plans. UPGRADE YOUR SHIP Earn money and score points by completing objectives and sinking enemies. Between missions, upgrade your hull, engine, weapons, damage control, smoke screen, and gunner systems. Higher-quality enemies are more dangerous, but grant greater rewards. Keep your remaining money to begin your next game with an advantage. LEARN AT YOUR OWN PACE A three-mission tutorial teaches you to navigate, aim, and survive. Read the manual and listen to every signal in the sound guide before entering combat. Play visually or through sound and VoiceOver. Choose from three difficulty levels: Deckhand, Captain, and Admiral. Complete as many missions as possible, keep your ship operational, and beat your best score. ---------- This app supports VoiceOver, Zoom, and other iOS accessibility features. If you encounter an accessibility problem, please contact us so we can fix it. Accessibility should be the foundation of a project, not a patch applied to the product.

en.title: Atomicom
en.summary: Space is young, dark and scattered. Atoms drift alone, touching nothing, and in all that emptiness not one thing has ever been built. No water. No stone. No star with a planet worth the name. That is what you are here to change. Atomicom is a puzzle game about binding matter together. Atoms come to you one at a time. Place them on the board, let their loose electrons find a partner, and when every electron in a connected group has one, the molecule is finished: it holds, it leaves the board, and the universe keeps a piece of itself that did not exist a moment ago. HOW IT PLAYS • An atom arrives in the glass cylinder below the board. Take it and drop it on any free square. • Atoms bond with the neighbours above, below, left and right of them. Never diagonally. • A green atom has one electron to give, yellow has two, orange three, red four. Blue atoms give nothing at all: they only take up room you were going to need. • Satisfy every electron in a connected group and the molecule forms and goes. • Run out of squares, or let the cylinder overflow, and the mission ends there. 300 MISSIONS The board starts wide and gets smaller: twelve squares across, then ten, then eight, then a six by six where there is nowhere left to be careless. Every mission asks more than the one before it — more molecules, more obstacles in the way, heavier atoms that need more neighbours before they are satisfied — and every time the board shrinks you begin again at something gentle and climb back up. MADE TO BE PLAYED BY EVERYONE Atomicom is made by Tyflos Accessible Software. Accessibility here is not a switch in the settings, it is how the game is built. • Fully playable with VoiceOver, from the first tap to the last molecule. Nothing has to be seen. • Every square tells you its coordinate, what is on it and how many electrons are still free: "A2, red, 3 free bonds". • The sound tells you where. An atom bonding on the left is heard on the left, and the top of the board sounds higher than the bottom, so the board has a shape you can hear. • Everything that happens without you touching it is spoken: an atom arriving, a molecule finished, a move the rules will not allow and why not. • Vibration answers every move, soft for an atom placed and hard for a molecule completed. • Drag if you like, or tap the atom and then the square. Both always work. • Dynamic Type throughout, and Reduce Motion and Reduce Transparency are obeyed. • Choose your own background, square borders and cylinder colour, and the game tells you when a colour you picked is too faint to make out. ALSO • Play in seventeen languages. • Made for iPhone and iPad. • Your game saves itself: leave in the middle of a mission and pick it up later. • A table of your best games, kept on your device. FREE, AND WHAT COSTS MONEY • The first ten missions are free, with advertising. • "All levels" is a one-off purchase that opens the three hundred. The advertising stays. • "No ads" is a second one-off purchase that removes the banner. It needs "All levels" first. The universe is not going to assemble itself. Start with two atoms.

HOW IT PLAYS • An atom arrives in the glass cylinder below the board. Take it and drop it on any free square. • Atoms bond with the neighbours above, below, left and right of them. Never diagonally. • A green atom has one electron to give, yellow has two, orange three, red four. Blue atoms give nothing at all: they only take up room you were going to need. • Satisfy every electron in a connected group and the molecule forms and goes. • Run out of squares, or let the cylinder overflow, and the mission ends there.

300 MISSIONS The board starts wide and gets smaller: twelve squares across, then ten, then eight, then a six by six where there is nowhere left to be careless. Every mission asks more than the one before it — more molecules, more obstacles in the way, heavier atoms that need more neighbours before they are satisfied — and every time the board shrinks you begin again at something gentle and climb back up.

MADE TO BE PLAYED BY EVERYONE Atomicom is made by Tyflos Accessible Software. Accessibility here is not a switch in the settings, it is how the game is built. • Fully playable with VoiceOver, from the first tap to the last molecule. Nothing has to be seen. • Every square tells you its coordinate, what is on it and how many electrons are still free: "A2, red, 3 free bonds". • The sound tells you where. An atom bonding on the left is heard on the left, and the top of the board sounds higher than the bottom, so the board has a shape you can hear. • Everything that happens without you touching it is spoken: an atom arriving, a molecule finished, a move the rules will not allow and why not. • Vibration answers every move, soft for an atom placed and hard for a molecule completed. • Drag if you like, or tap the atom and then the square. Both always work. • Dynamic Type throughout, and Reduce Motion and Reduce Transparency are obeyed. • Choose your own background, square borders and cylinder colour, and the game tells you when a colour you picked is too faint to make out.

ALSO • Play in seventeen languages. • Made for iPhone and iPad. • Your game saves itself: leave in the middle of a mission and pick it up later. • A table of your best games, kept on your device.

FREE, AND WHAT COSTS MONEY • The first ten missions are free, with advertising. • "All levels" is a one-off purchase that opens the three hundred. The advertising stays. • "No ads" is a second one-off purchase that removes the banner. It needs "All levels" first.

The universe is not going to assemble itself. Start with two atoms.

es.title: El audio espacial y los auriculares «open-ear» revolucionan la movilidad de las personas con discapacidad visual
es.summary: La unión entre el sonido binaural en 360 grados y los dispositivos de oído abierto resuelve uno de los mayores dilemas de la tiflotecnología. Gracias a este avance, las personas ciegas pueden recibir indicaciones GPS sin aislarse del ruido de la calle. Para una persona ciega o con baja visión, el oído funciona como un […] La entrada El audio espacial y los auriculares «open-ear» revolucionan la movilidad de las personas con discapacidad visual se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
La unión entre el sonido binaural en 360 grados y los dispositivos de oído abierto resuelve uno de los mayores dilemas de la tiflotecnología. Gracias a este avance, las personas ciegas pueden recibir indicaciones GPS sin aislarse del ruido de la calle.

Para una persona ciega o con baja visión, el oído funciona como un radar constante. Escuchar el tráfico, los pasos o el eco de las paredes resulta vital para caminar con seguridad. Sin embargo, usar el móvil o una aplicación GPS en la calle siempre obligaba a elegir entre dos malas opciones. Podías ponerte ambos auriculares y perder el contacto con el entorno, o llevar solo uno y sacrificar la orientación estéreo. Hoy, la combinación de audio espacial y auriculares open-ear acaba por fin con este dilema.

El audio espacial va mucho más allá del sonido estéreo tradicional. Mediante algoritmos binaurales y sensores de movimiento integrados en los auriculares, el sistema sitúa los sonidos en un espacio tridimensional de 360 grados alrededor del usuario.

Aplicaciones de navegación accesible como Soundscape Community o VoiceVista aprovechan esta tecnología para crear balizas sonoras virtuales. Por ejemplo, si tienes una cafetería o un paso de peatones a tu derecha, escucharás el aviso exactamente desde ese punto. Además, gracias al seguimiento dinámico de cabeza ( head tracking ), si giras el cuello para mirar hacia otro lado, el sonido permanece anclado en la ubicación física real.

La segunda pieza de esta revolución es el diseño de oído abierto ( open-ear ). A diferencia de los auriculares tradicionales de botón o de diadema cerrada, estos modelos dejan el canal auditivo completamente despejado. De este modo, el usuario percibe el sonido digital de su teléfono mezclado de forma natural con el ambiente de la calle.

Actualmente, existen tres formatos principales que compiten en el día a día de la comunidad ciega:

Conducción ósea: Dispositivos como los Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 transmiten el sonido mediante suaves vibraciones a través de los pómulos. Son extremadamente ligeros, resistentes al sudor y dejan el oído libre al cien por cien para la ecolocalización natural.

Conducción aérea direccional (OWS): Modelos como los Cleer ARC 5 , los Bose Ultra Open o los Shokz OpenFit colocan pequeños altavoces justo encima del canal auditivo. Ofrecen una calidad de graves superior y reproducen el audio espacial 3D con mucha mayor precisión.

Intraurales con modo transparencia: Auriculares como los AirPods Pro logran un audio espacial sobresaliente, pero recrean el sonido exterior mediante micrófonos. Aunque resultan muy eficaces, muchos usuarios prefieren la naturalidad de no llevar nada dentro del oído.

El impacto de combinar audio espacial y auriculares open-ear no se limita a los desplazamientos urbanos. En el ámbito deportivo, permite correr o entrenar siguiendo métricas por voz sin perder de vista el entorno.

Asimismo, el sector del gaming accesible está sacando un enorme partido a esta tecnología. Los audiogames y videojuegos con diseño sonoro 3D permiten identificar la posición exacta de enemigos, objetos o puertas mediante el sonido. Con unos buenos auriculares de oído abierto, disfrutar de estas experiencias resulta mucho más cómodo y evita la fatiga auditiva tras varias horas de uso.

Fuentes: Estudio sobre movilidad urbana y audio espacial en discapacidad visual , VoiceVista (ficha oficial en la App Store de Apple) ,

en.title: Top Tech Tidbits
en.summary: Top Tech Tidbits is a free weekly newsletter on access technology for people who are blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled. Founded in 2004 and read by over 48,000 people each week, it gathers human-curated news, tips and how-tos every Thursday morning. The app opens the newest issue the moment you open it, and keeps recent issues, and every older issue you open, on your iPhone and iPad, so you can read with no connection. MADE FOR BLIND AND LOW-VISION READERS FIRST • Built for VoiceOver and braille: every section and tidbit is a heading, every control is named, and Apple's accessibility audit checks every main screen in every version. • Larger Text up to the largest sizes, Light and Dark, Bold Text, the Atkinson Hyperlegible font, high-contrast colors and wider line spacing. • Listen: your iPhone reads the issue aloud in the voice and speed you choose, keeps reading when the screen locks, skips a whole section at a time, and stops on a sleep timer. Listen to all your saved tidbits in a row. • "Hey Siri, read me the latest Top Tech Tidbits" and "Hey Siri, search Top Tech Tidbits". • Keyboard commands for a keyboard connected to your iPhone or iPad. EVERY ISSUE SINCE 2008 • Past Issues lists this year's issues, then every earlier year back to 2008. • Search every issue from 2008 to today, tidbit by tidbit, even with no connection, and find tidbits from the iPhone's own search. • Topic Alerts: follow words or names, such as JAWS or braille, and get an alert when a new issue mentions them. Your iPhone looks through the issue itself, so your topics never reach us; only your own Apple devices and your iCloud account have them. • Events lists the upcoming events from the issues, soonest first; add any of them to your calendar in two taps. • A link to an issue, in an email or a message, opens right in the app at the tidbit it points to. • Stories open in Reader View: just their words, without the website's menus and ads. • Translate an issue into another language with Apple's own translation, on your device (iOS 18 or later). KEEP, NOTE AND SHARE • Save tidbits for later, add your own notes, and highlight passages; VoiceOver and braille say where each highlight starts and ends. All of it follows you to your other Apple devices through your iCloud account, with your settings and the place you left each issue. • Share any tidbit with a link that opens the issue right at it, or share a whole issue as a link, a text file or an EPUB book for the Books app or a braille notetaker. • Send Top Tech Tidbits a story from any app's Share button. ALWAYS THE NEWEST • An optional notification each Thursday, normally at 6:00 AM Eastern, with a Listen button; the issue is already downloaded, ready to read. A 1 on the app's icon means a new issue you have not opened yet. • Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, a Control Center button that starts Listen (iOS 18 or later), and shortcuts on the app's icon. • On iPad, the issue's sections or your saved tidbits sit beside the issue. PRIVACY No account, no advertising added by the app, and no tracking. To learn what readers find most useful the app keeps anonymous counts of which issues and tidbits are opened; you can turn them off in Settings. Details: https://toptechtidbits.com/app-privacy/ Questions and ideas: publisher@toptechtidbits.com

en.title: I Have a Garden
en.summary: One zucchini plant. 48 real days. Here the game's time is your time. You water it tonight and by tomorrow the soil will be a little drier. It gets light and dark at the same time as it does outside your window. The stems, the leaves and the flowers are drawn by an algorithm that imitates how a plant really grows. No two games give you the same shape, or the same harvest. Once you have the zucchini figured out, try the tomato plant: twice the days, up to twenty tomatoes, suckers to prune and a plant that climbs tied to its stake. It brings its own seeds, its own chimera tomato and new achievements. And for a third challenge, the pepper plant: 72 days, and snails that climb the stem to eat its leaves and peppers, which you pick off with your gloves. Each pepper turns from green to yellow to red, and you have to pick it at the right moment. It brings its own chimera pepper, its own seeds and new achievements. You unlock it with a single purchase, which also removes the ads. All three plants grow at the same time, each in its own plot. WHAT YOU'LL DO You check on it, water or feed it if it's time, look for pests and pull the odd weed. For as long as you feel like. HOW THE CYCLE GOES You start by preparing the soil and burying the seed. Until flowering you have to look after it as well as you can, because that stretch decides how many flowers open. When they do, the bees arrive to pollinate them, and if you've kept it up, every one sets fruit. The last stretch takes the most attention: each zucchini has its right moment, and picking it early or leaving it too long costs you points. IMPROVE YOUR PLANT When the cycle ends, you can take the seeds out of the Prime and Overripe zucchini you harvested. There are four qualities: Wild, Adapted, Selected and Heirloom. The better the seed, the more main branches the stem puts out. That raises your chances of getting a chimera zucchini, the hardest thing in the game to pull off. ACHIEVEMENTS There are twenty-seven achievements to earn along the way, gardener's ranks among them: when you gather the harvest you get a score and the rank you earned with the plant. WHAT IT DOESN'T DO No account, no email. No lives, no paying your way forward: the only purchase is the pepper plant, and it's optional. No leaderboard, nobody to beat. And it doesn't message you for the sake of it: a notification arrives when the plant actually needs something, at most one a day, not every evening at seven. It's free and kept going by advertising. If you'd rather support it another way, the pepper purchase removes the ads for good. ALSO You can put a widget on your home screen with the water and feed gauges, without opening the game. A notebook inside that explains every mechanic with real numbers, if you want to know why. A daily graph of water, feed and pests since the day you planted the seed. And a few more surprises. Thank you for playing.

en.title: ScribbleGrid: Word Search
en.summary: Word search at its most satisfying! Read the clue, figure out the word, then swipe across the grid to find it. Every word you find reveals a letter of the Secret Word — crack it before you finish the grid! THE SECRET WORD: A NEW LAYER ON WORD SEARCH Every puzzle hides a Secret Word. Each word you find reveals one of its letters. Guess it before the grid is done: the earlier you crack it, the bigger the bonus. You get 3 guesses! DAILY PUZZLE One puzzle a day, the same for everyone — including the same Secret Word. Keep your streak, share your result with a spoiler-free emoji card and climb the daily Game Center leaderboard. NO WORD LIST, JUST CLUES The words aren't handed to you — you work them out from clues. They hide horizontally, vertically, diagonally, even backwards. PLAY WITH VOICEOVER ScribbleGrid can be played from start to finish with VoiceOver. Clues and grid letters are read aloud; mark a word by double-tapping its first and last letters. Hear a whole row, column or diagonal at once, and hear every letter as you type the Secret Word. A step-by-step VoiceOver guide is built into the game. COMBO SCORING Find words within 10 seconds of each other to push your multiplier up to x5. THREE DIFFICULTY LEVELS Easy: short words, straight directions. Medium: reversed directions join in. Hard: long words in all 8 directions. STATS AND STREAK REMINDERS Track your streak, best times and solved Secret Words. If the puzzle is still waiting, get an optional reminder at 8 PM. TWO LANGUAGES, THOUSANDS OF WORDS Thousands of carefully written clues in English and Turkish. Great for language learners too. PLAY ANYWHERE A 10x10 grid on iPhone, a huge 15x15 grid on iPad. No internet needed — play on a plane, on the subway, anywhere. NO ADS There are no ads in the game. ScribbleGrid Pro adds unlimited hints, 2x coin rewards and instant solve in classic mode — a one-time purchase, no subscription. If you love word games, puzzles and brain teasers, ScribbleGrid is made for you. Download now and crack today's Secret Word!

es.title: IrisVision Ultra: unas nuevas gafas inteligentes amplían la visión hasta 10 aumentos con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial
es.summary: La compañía IrisVision presenta un nuevo dispositivo electrónico para personas con baja visión. Incorpora enfoque automático, diferentes modos de visualización y un asistente de inteligencia artificial capaz de leer textos y adaptar la imagen a las necesidades del usuario. La tecnología continúa ofreciendo nuevas alternativas para las personas con discapacidad visual. Una de las últimas […] La entrada IrisVision Ultra: unas nuevas gafas inteligentes amplían la visión hasta 10 aumentos con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
La compañía IrisVision presenta un nuevo dispositivo electrónico para personas con baja visión. Incorpora enfoque automático, diferentes modos de visualización y un asistente de inteligencia artificial capaz de leer textos y adaptar la imagen a las necesidades del usuario.

La tecnología continúa ofreciendo nuevas alternativas para las personas con discapacidad visual. Una de las últimas novedades llega de la mano de IrisVision, que ha presentado sus nuevas IrisVision Ultra , unas gafas electrónicas diseñadas para facilitar actividades cotidianas como leer, reconocer rostros, ver la televisión o consultar información a distancia.

Uno de los principales atractivos de las IrisVision Ultra es su capacidad de ampliación. El dispositivo permite aumentar la imagen hasta 10 veces y cuenta con un sistema de enfoque automático que mantiene la nitidez al observar objetos a diferentes distancias.

Esto permite utilizar las gafas para distintas actividades, tanto de cerca como a distancias intermedias o lejanas.

Además, incorporan varios modos de visualización para adaptar la imagen a diferentes necesidades:

También incluyen un modo específico para televisión, que ajusta la exposición para reducir los reflejos y mejorar la visualización de los contenidos.

Otra de las novedades es la integración de Iris, la plataforma de inteligencia artificial de IrisVision.

Este asistente permite controlar diferentes funciones mediante comandos de voz. El usuario puede solicitar que aumente la imagen, modifique el brillo, cambie el contraste o active un modo de lectura.

Una de sus funciones más interesantes es la lectura de textos en voz alta. Basta con dirigir la mirada hacia una página, una etiqueta o una carta para pedirle a Iris que lea su contenido.

El sistema admite 14 idiomas, entre ellos el español, y permite interactuar con las gafas utilizando instrucciones sencillas.

La inteligencia artificial también facilita el acceso a otros contenidos. Por ejemplo, permite buscar vídeos en YouTube, consultar películas, escuchar audiolibros y acceder a juegos diseñados específicamente para personas con baja visión.

Las IrisVision Ultra pesan aproximadamente 230 gramos y ofrecen una autonomía de hasta 10 horas, según las condiciones de uso y la configuración del dispositivo.

Una de sus novedades es la incorporación de botones táctiles directamente en las gafas. Gracias a ellos, el usuario puede desplazarse por los diferentes modos, modificar los aumentos y controlar las funciones sin necesidad de manejar un mando independiente.

Esta característica resulta especialmente interesante desde el punto de vista de la accesibilidad, ya que permite localizar los controles mediante el tacto.

Además, cada dispositivo incluye una sesión individual de formación a distancia para ayudar al usuario a familiarizarse con sus funciones.

IrisVision presenta este dispositivo como una ayuda electrónica para personas con diferentes patologías visuales.

Entre los perfiles a los que se dirige se encuentran personas con:

Las diferentes opciones de ampliación, contraste y adaptación del campo visual permiten personalizar la experiencia según las necesidades de cada persona.

No obstante, estas gafas no son una solución universal. Su utilidad depende del resto visual, las características de cada patología y las necesidades concretas del usuario. Por eso, es recomendable probar el dispositivo y contar con asesoramiento especializado en baja visión antes de adquirirlo.

El precio es uno de los aspectos más importantes de este lanzamiento.

Según la página oficial del fabricante, las IrisVision Ultra tienen un precio promocional de 3.799 dólares , frente a los 3.999 dólares de su precio original.

Al cambio aproximado, esta cantidad equivale a unos 3.460 euros. Sin embargo, hay que tener en cuenta que se trata de una conversión orientativa y que el precio final para compradores europeos puede variar.

La compañía indica además un coste de envío internacional de 135 dólares. A esta cantidad podrían añadirse impuestos y otros gastos de importación, por lo que conviene consultar las condiciones antes de realizar el pedido.

Por el momento, el fabricante comercializa el dispositivo directamente desde su página web.

Las IrisVision Ultra representan una nueva apuesta por las ayudas electrónicas portátiles para personas con baja visión.

Su combinación de ampliación de imagen, ajustes de contraste, lectura de textos e inteligencia artificial busca facilitar actividades cotidianas que pueden resultar complicadas cuando existe una pérdida de visión.

Aunque su precio sigue siendo elevado y será necesario conocer la experiencia de los usuarios con este nuevo modelo, el dispositivo muestra cómo la tecnología puede ofrecer herramientas cada vez más personalizadas para aprovechar el resto visual.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuente: Iris Vision

en.title: From TalkBack to Jieshuo, and Now SandFly: My Journey Through Android Screen Readers
en.summary: After years of using TalkBack and Jieshuo, I’ve decided to make SandFly my primary screen reader. For me, this isn’t simply about replacing one application…
en.body:
Published 18 November 2026 by Salih Kunduz

After years of using TalkBack and Jieshuo, I’ve decided to make SandFly my primary screen reader.

For me, this isn’t simply about replacing one application with another. It’s also an opportunity to look back at how Android accessibility has evolved over the years, what we’ve gained along the way, and what I expect from a screen reader today.

I’ve been using Android for a long time, and I’ve witnessed quite a few changes in its accessibility ecosystem. Some were genuinely exciting, while others reminded us how limited our choices were.

Table of Contents

For much of the period between 2013 and 2020, TalkBack was practically the only realistic option for many blind Android users.

There were other attempts and alternatives, of course, but TalkBack dominated the ecosystem. It came with Google’s backing, was integrated into Android, and worked across a wide range of devices.

I don’t want to underestimate what TalkBack meant to us during those years. It made Android usable for millions of blind people, including me. It improved considerably over time, and many features we take for granted today were not available in its earlier versions.

However, there was always something that bothered me: performance.

TalkBack often felt heavier and slower than it needed to be. Navigating through interfaces, moving between elements, and performing everyday tasks sometimes required more patience than I thought was reasonable.

And when you use a screen reader for practically everything you do on your phone, these small delays add up.

The problem wasn’t simply that TalkBack was slow. It was that we had very little choice. If something didn’t work the way we wanted, we could report it, wait for an update, or learn to live with it.

For years, that was simply the reality of Android accessibility.

My experience with Jieshuo changed the way I thought about screen readers.

For the first time, I felt that I was getting much closer to the full performance of my Android device.

The difference wasn’t limited to speech responsiveness. Navigation felt faster, interactions were more immediate, and I had considerably more control over how my screen reader behaved.

Jieshuo offered a level of customization that TalkBack had never really provided. I could adjust the experience to suit my habits rather than constantly adapting my habits to the screen reader.

Once you become accustomed to that level of responsiveness and flexibility, going back isn’t easy.

But Jieshuo had its own problems.

One of the biggest challenges was communication with its developer. When something didn’t work properly, reporting an issue and getting meaningful feedback wasn’t always straightforward. For a product that plays such an important role in our daily lives, communication matters enormously.

There was also the issue of distribution and compatibility.

Because Jieshuo wasn’t available through Google Play, certain banking applications and other security-sensitive services occasionally created problems. Some applications treated the screen reader as a potential security risk, even though we were simply using it to access our devices.

As a blind user, I found that particularly frustrating.

A screen reader isn’t an optional convenience. It’s the interface through which we interact with our phones. Having to choose between using the screen reader I prefer and accessing essential services is not a reasonable situation.

And then there were the practical complications. Even something as ordinary as paying for a screen reader could involve additional services, intermediaries, or procedures that an average user shouldn’t have to deal with.

These things might seem relatively minor when considered separately, but together they affect the overall experience.

Jieshuo showed me what was possible in terms of performance and customization. At the same time, it made me appreciate certain advantages I had previously taken for granted.

Despite all my criticism of TalkBack’s performance, I never completely abandoned it.

There was something reassuring about knowing it was there.

TalkBack was officially supported, widely recognized, and generally less likely to create complications with applications that were sensitive to accessibility services.

Whenever I encountered a problem with Jieshuo, I knew I could return to TalkBack.

It might not have been as fast or as flexible as I wanted, but it provided a familiar and relatively predictable experience.

In that sense, TalkBack became my safe harbor.

And I think that says something important about screen readers. Performance matters, but so do stability, reliability, compatibility, and trust.

The ideal screen reader shouldn’t force us to sacrifice one for another.

After all these years, I think we need to reconsider what we actually expect from an Android screen reader.

Of course, responsiveness and advanced features matter. Nobody wants to use a slow or unnecessarily restrictive screen reader.

But speed alone isn’t enough.

A screen reader should be stable, reliable, and inclusive. It should be easy to obtain, straightforward to set up, and accessible to people with different levels of technical experience.

You shouldn’t need a master’s degree, let alone a PhD in technology, just to configure your screen reader and use your phone comfortably.

I enjoy experimenting with technology. I don’t mind exploring advanced settings, testing new features, or finding workarounds when something doesn’t behave as expected.

But that’s my personal interest. It shouldn’t be a requirement for everyone else.

Someone who has just started using Android with a screen reader should be able to learn the basics without feeling overwhelmed. Meanwhile, experienced users should have access to the advanced tools and customization they need.

These two expectations aren’t contradictory.

A well-designed screen reader should be approachable for beginners without becoming restrictive for advanced users.

Accessibility must extend beyond the application’s interface, too. Installation, updates, payments, documentation, and communication with developers are all part of the experience.

If obtaining or paying for an accessibility tool requires navigating through several third-party services and complicated procedures, then something is wrong with that experience.

These considerations have become increasingly important to me, and they’re among the reasons I’ve started looking at SandFly more seriously.

What initially attracted me to SandFly was its approach.

Because SandFly builds on TalkBack’s foundation, many aspects of the experience already feel familiar. Its settings, menus, and general structure don’t require me to forget years of accumulated habits and start from scratch.

That’s a significant advantage.

Changing screen readers isn’t always easy, particularly when you’ve spent years developing your own gestures, routines, and ways of interacting with Android.

With SandFly, I feel that I’m getting something close to the safety and familiarity of TalkBack, combined with a much more capable and comfortable environment.

If TalkBack was my safe harbor, SandFly feels like that same harbor opening into a much more luxurious bay.

It’s a slightly unusual comparison, perhaps, but it describes the feeling quite well.

The familiar foundation is still there, while the possibilities continue to expand.

SandFly is still a developing project, and I don’t want to pretend that every feature is perfect or that it has already solved every problem. However, its advanced capabilities are progressing, and I’ve been encouraged by the direction of its development.

Another important advantage is how approachable the experience feels.

I don’t have to spend hours trying to understand an entirely unfamiliar system just to configure the basics. At the same time, there are more advanced possibilities to explore as I become accustomed to it.

That balance is exactly what I want from a modern screen reader.

There are also some very practical reasons behind my decision.

First, paying for the software doesn’t have to become a separate technical challenge. If I decide to purchase it, I don’t have to deal with numerous intermediary services just to complete the process.

That might not sound particularly exciting, but simplicity matters.

Second, SandFly hasn’t caused problems with the banking service I personally use.

I want to be careful about how I describe this. My experience doesn’t mean every banking application will necessarily work without issues for every user. But for me, being able to use my preferred screen reader without compromising access to an essential financial service is a major advantage.

And then there’s something that deserves more attention: physical keyboards.

SandFly appears to place considerable importance on physical keyboard support, and it’s clear that thought has gone into this part of the experience.

This matters to me personally because I don’t use Android exclusively on a phone. I also use a tablet, and physical keyboard interaction is an important part of how I work with it.

A screen reader that treats physical keyboard navigation as a serious part of the user experience, rather than an afterthought, immediately becomes more interesting to me.

I don’t think physical keyboard support receives enough attention in discussions about Android accessibility.

We often focus on touch gestures, speech responsiveness, and customization. Those are important, of course, but Android is no longer limited to the traditional smartphone experience.

Tablets, foldables, keyboards, and different ways of interacting with our devices deserve equal consideration.

The more I explored SandFly from this perspective, the more I began to feel that it could become a screen reader I would genuinely enjoy using every day.

There’s another factor that has influenced my decision: communication with the developer.

After my experience with Jieshuo, I have come to value this much more than I used to.

Being able to contact a developer, explain a problem, discuss an idea, and receive feedback makes a real difference.

This doesn’t mean every suggestion should be accepted or every bug should be fixed immediately. Software development doesn’t work that way.

What matters is knowing that communication is possible and that users’ experiences are being considered.

Through my work with Accessible Android, I’ve spent a considerable amount of time testing applications, reporting accessibility issues, and communicating with developers.

One thing I’ve learned is that the relationship between developers and users can influence the quality of a product just as much as technical decisions do.

SandFly’s developer has been approachable, and that gives me another reason to follow the project closely.

Of course, good communication alone doesn’t guarantee good software. The product still has to demonstrate its reliability through daily use.

But when a project combines technical ambition with an approachable developer, I’m much more willing to invest my time in it.

I’m not switching to SandFly because I believe TalkBack has become irrelevant or because I want to dismiss everything Jieshuo has offered me.

Quite the opposite.

I appreciate what both screen readers have contributed to my Android experience.

Without TalkBack, my early years on Android would have been very different. Without Jieshuo, I might never have realized how much faster and more flexible screen reading could feel.

But I’m also not particularly interested in remaining loyal to a screen reader simply because I’ve used it for years.

My loyalty is to accessibility, independence, and the freedom to use technology in the way that suits me best.

SandFly will have to prove itself through everyday use. There will almost certainly be bugs, missing features, and situations where I may need to return to another screen reader.

That’s perfectly normal for a developing project.

For now, however, I see enough potential to make the transition.

What I find particularly encouraging is that we seem to be moving toward a more diverse Android accessibility ecosystem.

We no longer have to evaluate screen readers solely in terms of whether they can read an interface. We can discuss performance, usability, reliability, physical keyboard support, distribution, payment accessibility, developer communication, and the overall quality of the experience.

And we should.

After all, an Android screen reader shouldn’t simply make a device accessible.

It should make using that device comfortable, efficient, and enjoyable.

That’s what I’m looking for in SandFly, and that’s why I’ve decided to give it a chance.
